messages.author: fbff4100433066b4
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Variable Transformation
parts:
I am running a lagged regression and my multiplier estimate in a regression like this:

y = X\beta + eps

is sum(beta).

So I can either have my parameter as a vector beta and a generated quantity sum(beta) or I can factor the vector beta into two parameters 1) a simplex lambda and a multiplier m.
This way lambda is the shape (distribution of beta across different lags) and m is sum(beta). The factored approach also allow you to put a single prior on m.

Its gets more complicated when in a single hierarchical model you have many m's (that draw from common distribution) but they all share the same lambda. I have not been able to work out the Jacobian for this case yet. I think in this case the variable transformation is not a bijection.

regards,
vishy

intermediate space and then marginalize out the excess parameter.
See https://arxiv.org/abs/1010.3436.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Variable Transformation
parts:
> On Jan 26, 2017, at 12:40 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> The simplex transform is not a bijection. You have to do a 1-1 to an
> intermediate space and then marginalize out the excess parameter.
> See https://arxiv.org/abs/1010.3436.

I'm pretty sure the simplex transform we use in Stan is a a bijection
(one-to-one and onto) from unit K-simplexes to R^(K-1).

I think Vishv's transform took account of that by only using (K-1)
components of the simplex.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Variable Transformation
parts: > On Jan 26, 2017, at 9:49 AM, Vishv Jeet <vishv...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I am running a lagged regression and my multiplier estimate in a regression like this:
>
> y = X\beta + eps
>
> is sum(beta).

What's a "multiplier estimate"? Does sum(beta) play a role in
the model?
> So I can either have my parameter as a vector beta and a generated quantity sum(beta) or I can factor the vector beta into two parameters 1) a simplex lambda and a multiplier m.

This keeps things positive (assuming m is constrained to be positive).

But if you put the priors on m and on the simplex, then you
use a function of the two results, you don't need the
Jacobian adjustment in Stan. You only need the Jacobian if
you want to put a distribution on the transformed variable.
> This way lambda is the shape (distribution of beta across different lags) and m is sum(beta). The factored approach also allow you to put a single prior on m.

Right. We do the same thing with Dirichlet priors, decomposing
them into a total prior count and a simplex.

> Its gets more complicated when in a single hierarchical model you have many m's (that draw from common distribution) but they all share the same lambda. I have not been able to work out the Jacobian for this case yet. I think in this case the variable transformation is not a bijection.

You just drop all the redundant components. So if there are J groups
with their own m and a single K-simplex, the basis is (J + K - 1) degrees
of freedom.

- Bob

messages.author: fbff4100433066b4
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Variable Transformation
parts:
That is because simplex has only K-1 degree of freedom, and to compensate for that I had m.

(m lambda_1, lambda_2, ..., lambda_K-1) -> (beta_1, beta_2, ..., beta_K)

with

beta_K -> m * (1 - sum(i \in 1:K-1, lambda_i))

regards,
Vishy
